title: A Smile for the Hymn
premise: Elodie Ishikawa, a rationalist pest controller, is hired to clear 'vermin' from a derelict farmhouse where every mirror shows an extra chair and every photograph of her late grandmother's house has gained one too. The vermin are people — hollowed, smiling remnants of a congregation that vanished in 1962 after singing the final verse of a harvest hymn. The hymn's composer, a preacher who traded his congregation's souls for his own survival, still collects a tithe each harvest moon, and Elodie's grandmother was the one who escaped mid-song, leaving the last verse unfinished. To end the cycle, Elodie must learn the verse from the dead without letting it finish inside her, then sing it back at its source before the moon rises — a choice that costs her either her voice, her memories of everyone she loves, or the life of the last living member of the congregation. She survives by refusing to sing alone: she teaches the verse to the hollowed dead, and they finish it together, unmaking the preacher but leaving Elodie with a smile she cannot explain and a chair in every photograph that now, finally, is empty.
about_author: Noor Ishikawa is a former archivist of regional hymnals who grew up between Osaka and rural Vermont, where harvest festivals were held in churches that no longer had congregations. Her fiction explores what survives of faith when only the songs remain.

chapters.title: The Callout
chapters.summary: Elodie's POV. A routine pest-control call at the Hollis farmhouse turns strange: droppings arranged in rows, walls warm like held breath, and a hymnal nailed shut in the pantry. Elodie documents everything clinically, refusing the client's whispered warnings. Emotional beat: competent skepticism curdling into unease.

chapters.title: Fingerprints
chapters.summary: Elodie's POV. She finds handprints on the inside of a sealed chimney — small, adult, pressed outward. Her rational explanations stack and fail one by one. That night she photographs her grandmother's old house for insurance and notices, for the first time, a wooden chair in the corner of every frame. Beat: denial cracking.

chapters.title: The Extra Chair
chapters.summary: Alternating POV with her brother Marcus. The chair appears in family photos spanning decades, always in the corner, always facing the camera. Marcus, who believed in grandma's stories, begs Elodie to leave it alone. She burns the prints instead. Beat: sibling fracture; the house answers with a knock.

chapters.title: Hollow Congregation
chapters.summary: Elodie's POV. Returning to the farmhouse at dusk, she finds the 'vermin': seven figures standing in the pews of a collapsed chapel annex, smiling, unmoving, their eyes like developed film. One turns its head toward her and mouths a word she refuses to read. Beat: terror held at arm's length.

chapters.title: What Grandma Kept
chapters.summary: Marcus's POV. He opens grandma's locked cedar chest: the same hymnal, unnailed, its last page torn out, and a letter beginning 'If you are reading this, the chair has found you.' He drives to Elodie's apartment through streets where every church bell rings one note. Beat: dread inherited.

chapters.title: The Tithe
chapters.summary: Elodie's POV. She learns the pattern: every harvest moon, someone in the county vanishes, and the seven smile a little wider. A county archive photo from 1962 shows the congregation — eight members. The eighth is her grandmother. Beat: personal stakes ignite.

chapters.title: Preacher Voss
chapters.summary: Archive interlude, 1961–62 documents and a dying deacon's testimony. Reverend Amos Voss promised his flock deliverance from a blight year; the hymn's final verse was a contract. He alone walked out of the chapel. Beat: the horror has an author, and he is still hungry.

chapters.title: Verse One Through Five
chapters.summary: Elodie's POV. She transcribes the surviving verses; singing them aloud makes the room's temperature drop and her reflection lag. Marcus arrives with the chest. They fight about belief, about grandma, about who gets to decide what Elodie risks. Beat: alliance reforged through anger.

chapters.title: The Hollow Speak
chapters.summary: Elodie's POV, night vigil in the farmhouse. The seven don't attack; they wait, and when she hums, their smiles twitch with longing. One — a girl in a 1960s dress — scratches a word into the dust: ALMOST. Beat: the monsters are victims, and it is worse.

chapters.title: Moonrise Rehearsal
chapters.summary: Marcus's POV. First harvest moon approaches. They rehearse the hymn with the torn verse missing; each run-through, the chair in the photographs moves closer to the camera. Elodie's hands begin moving on their own, conducting. Beat: the song is already in her.

chapters.title: The Deacon's Granddaughter
chapters.summary: Elodie's POV. She tracks down Ruth, the deacon's granddaughter, the last living witness, now ninety and lucid only at dusk. Ruth describes the final verse — not its words, but the sensation of almost finishing it, and what it cost her father. Beat: warning as inheritance.

chapters.title: Ruth's Bargain
chapters.summary: Ruth's POV. She offers Elodie the torn page, kept in a Bible hollowed like a reliquary, for one promise: that the verse, once learned, dies with its singer. Elodie agrees, lying. Ruth knows. She gives it anyway. Beat: complicity passed like a torch.

chapters.title: Learning It
chapters.summary: Elodie's POV. Alone, she reads the final verse once. It is beautiful in the way a trap is beautiful. She does not sing it, but it sings itself in her dreams, in grandma's voice, one word further each night. Beat: infection by melody.

chapters.title: The Chair Arrives
chapters.summary: Marcus's POV. The chair is now in the room with them — physical, smelling of varnish and cold earth, facing Elodie's bed. Neighbors report hymn-singing from the vacant apartment above. Elodie wakes with her lips moving. Beat: the boundary between song and self collapses.

chapters.title: What Voss Wants
chapters.summary: Elodie's POV. She finally understands the mechanism: Voss doesn't collect souls; he collects unfinished songs, and the harvest moon is when the contract comes due for renewal. He needs a voice willing to finish the verse in his place. Grandma escaped mid-note; the debt rolled down. Beat: the trap's full shape.

chapters.title: Sixteen Smiles
chapters.summary: Elodie and Marcus, shared POV. The seven have become sixteen; the farmhouse chapel is full now, pews packed with the smiling. The girl in the dust writes HELP US FINISH. Elodie realizes the dead don't want release from the song — they want release through it. Beat: moral inversion, plan forming.

chapters.title: The Night Before
chapters.summary: Marcus's POV. Quiet chapter: repairs, confessions, grandma's letters read aloud. Elodie admits she's not sure she'll be able to stop singing. Marcus offers to finish it in her place; she refuses, and for the first time says thank you instead of I don't need you. Beat: love stated plainly before the dark.

chapters.title: Harvest Moon
chapters.summary: Elodie's POV. She enters the chapel at moonrise, hymnal open, Voss waiting in the pulpit — not decayed, but polished, like furniture kept in a good house. The congregation turns as one. He offers her the deal he offered grandma: sing the verse, live, forget. Beat: the devil's terms, sincerely meant.

chapters.title: The Last Verse
chapters.summary: Elodie's POV, climax. She begins to sing — and cannot stop, the verse pulling itself out of her. At the final line she does the one thing Voss never planned for: she stops singing and lets the sixteen finish it together, a chord of the hollowed dead. Voss unravels into sheet music and dust. Beat: triumph through surrender of control.

chapters.title: Aftermath
chapters.summary: Marcus's POV. The chapel is empty, warm, ordinary. The photographs lose the chair. But Elodie hasn't spoken since the moon set — the verse took her voice as its price, exactly as Ruth promised. Beat: victory with a bill attached.

chapters.title: The Price of Survival
chapters.summary: Elodie's POV, mute, weeks later. She returns to pest control, communicating by notepad, oddly at peace. Ruth dies smiling; at the funeral, Elodie hums — one note, hers, unclaimed. The dead are free; the debt is paid in a currency she chose. Beat: grief transmuted into ownership of the cost.

chapters.title: A Smile for the Hymn
chapters.summary: Elodie's POV, coda. At grandma's house, sold now, she finds one last photograph in the wall: grandma mid-escape, 1962, looking directly at the camera — and smiling. Not in terror. In hope that someone would finish it right. Elodie smiles back, voiceless, and closes the album. Beat: haunted, but no longer hunted; a final image that is blessing and warning at once.
